scenes.name: 1966: el año del single
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: El libro son doce ensayos, uno por mes, cada uno a partir de un single. 1966 fue el último año en que el 45 fue la forma principal del pop, antes de que Sgt. Pepper’s convirtiera el LP en la fuerza creativa y comercial en el verano de 1967: en dos o tres minutos cabían ideas, actitudes, letras y experimentos que después se estirarían en álbumes de cuarenta minutos. El pop dejó de ser comercio, romance adolescente o diversión para volverse una experiencia total, «la única cosa viva» según Lou Reed, y el prisma con el que se interpretaba el mundo. El año empezó en el pop y acabó en el rock; empezó en la Gran Sociedad de Johnson y acabó con el resurgir republicano. Hubo ambición, aceleración y compresión, y una reacción proporcional de quienes veían que todo cambiaba demasiado deprisa. Savage, que cumplió trece años ese verano escuchando Radio Caroline South, se ciñe a los singles, sobre todo los que entraron en las listas de Billboard y Record Retailer, y deja fuera el free jazz, el minimalismo, el ska, los happenings y los situacionistas.
scenes.family: Juventud, moda y medios: Swinging London, radio pirata

scenes.name: The Beatles
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Su primer single, «Love Me Do», entró en las listas el 11 de octubre de 1962, días antes de la crisis de los misiles. En 1963 provocaron una histeria femenina sin precedentes, rompieron la deferencia de los cincuenta y, por un breve tiempo, el sistema de clases: una revolución hecha con una melodía, un flequillo y un «yeah yeah yeah». En abril de 1964 ocuparon los cinco primeros puestos de Billboard, dispararon la venta de singles y convirtieron Gran Bretaña en la «Isla Pop». Su ejemplo obligaba a componer material propio. En 1966 hay pausas súbitas dentro del impulso imparable de «Rain».

scenes.name: Alicia, la locura y el regreso a la infancia
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: Al final de 1966 el LSD llevó al pop de vuelta a la infancia y a la locura. Los Beatles empezaron el 24 de noviembre «Strawberry Fields Forever», un viaje de Lennon hacia abajo, no hacia atrás, al orfanato junto a su casa, «psicoanálisis con música», unida por Geoff Emerick a partir de dos tomas; luego «When I’m Sixty-Four» y «Penny Lane». En Navidad la BBC aplazó el Alice in Wonderland de Jonathan Miller, sin cabezas de animal, con el sitar de Ravi Shankar y rodado en un hospital militar de víctimas de neurosis de guerra: un catálogo de psicosis. Grace Slick llevó «White Rabbit» a Jefferson Airplane; Syd Barrett escribía sobre el mundo de Lewis Carroll. Proliferaban los discos sobre la locura («They’re Coming to Take Me Away, Ha-Haaa!», «Pandora’s Golden Heebie Jeebies» de los Association), y en el corazón secreto del año, la tristeza frágil de «How Can We Hang On to a Dream» de Tim Hardin.

scenes.name: Contracultura, Sgt. Pepper y Woodstock
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: La revolución negra sacudió también a la juventud blanca: la cuestión moral de los derechos civiles, el racismo familiar, la atracción por la cultura negra, el miedo al reclutamiento y las drogas. Dylan y los Beatles convirtieron el rock en forma de vida. Sgt. Pepper (1967), de unos Beatles criados con Chuck Berry («a mí no me ha pasado nada desde 1958, cuando oí el rock and roll negro», dijo Lennon), abrió la era psicodélica que influiría en Electric Ladyland de Hendrix y en el Free Your Mind… de Funkadelic; Sly salió en el Ed Sullivan con uniforme de banda, y de ahí viene el púrpura de Prince. La contracultura sintetizó jazz, R&B, pop, rock y folk en formas largas, espectáculos de luces y tecnología, rasgos que el black rock (Hendrix, Sly, Funkadelic, War, Ohio Players, los Isley, Bar-Kays) llevó al funk. En Woodstock (1969) brillaron Hendrix, Sly y Santana. Las muertes de Hendrix, Joplin y Morrison, Altamont, Kent State y Jackson State acabaron con la idea de que el rock cambiaría el mundo; en la música negra el funk mantuvo vivos esos ideales.

podcast.title: Exemption from National Service (1957)
podcast.body: John Lennon, born in October 1940, was exempt from compulsory national service in Britain. The obligation officially ended in 1957 for anyone born on or after October 1, 1939, allowing him to pursue his musical career without military interruption. "And Lenin was born in October 1940, so he's great-bite."

podcast.title: "More Popular Than Jesus" Comment (1966)
podcast.body: In 1966, John Lennon made a controversial remark claiming that The Beatles were "more popular than Jesus." This comment was considered blasphemous by broadcasters Tommy Charles and Doug Layton in Birmingham, Alabama, who subsequently launched a campaign to ban The Beatles, resulting in public record destruction. "And when John Lennon made a flippin' comment in 1966 about the Beatles being more popular than Jesus, two broadcasters, Tommy Charles and Doug Layton from Birmingham, Alabama, started a campaign to ban the Beatles over this blasphemy, and many records were broken and burned."

podcast.title: Immigration Issues and Marijuana Conviction (1968/1972)
podcast.body: John Lennon faced significant immigration challenges in the United States due to a marijuana conviction in England in 1968. This conviction was used by the US government as a reason to attempt his deportation, initiated in part by South Carolina Senator Strom Thurmond. This legal battle tied Lennon up in immigration court for a year and a half, preventing his planned anti-Nixon tour. "Lennon was not permitted into the country. He had a little bit of a problem with a previous arrest due to possession of marijuana."

podcast.title: Bahamas Attempt (1969)
podcast.body: Prior to the Montreal bed-in, John Lennon and Yoko Ono intended to host the event in the Bahamas. They flew there on May 24, 1969, but only spent one night because of the oppressive heat, leading them to seek an alternative location in Canada. "They then intended to host the event in the Bahamas, but after flying in on May 24th, 1969, they only spent one night there because of the heat."

podcast.title: Bed-Ins for Peace (1969)
podcast.body: As a form of peace protest, John and Yoko Ono staged "bed-ins" where they remained in bed for a week, giving interviews about peace. They first held one in Amsterdam and then another in Montreal. They were denied entry into New York to stage a third due to Lennon's prior marijuana arrest, but Lennon stated the "silly" nature was intentional for the protest. "It was essentially John and Yoko in bed for a week, giving interviews about peace."

podcast.body: John Lennon's famous "Bed-Ins for Peace" in 1969 were referenced in his memoirs by the quote, "trying to start a revolution from me bed." This phrase, from a bootlegged tape of his memoirs, deeply impressed Noel Gallagher and provided inspiration for Oasis' "Don't Look Back In Anger." "He was particularly impressed by this quote from Lenin, trying to start a revolution from me bed, referring to his famous Beddins for Peace, back in 1969."

podcast.title: Bed-Ins for Peace (1969)
podcast.body: John Lennon and his partner Yoko Ono held a week-long non-violent "bed-in for peace" protest in Montreal from May 26 to June 1, 1969. Intended as a novel way to promote peace against the Vietnam War, this event followed an earlier bed-in in Amsterdam, and was planned for Montreal after Lennon was denied entry to the United States due to a 1968 cannabis conviction and a brief, uncomfortable stay in the Bahamas due to heat. "On May 26th, June 1st, 1969, he held a bed in for peace protest in Montreal."

podcast.title: Canadian Visa and Hotel Choices (1969)
podcast.body: After the Bahamas attempt, John Lennon and Yoko Ono landed in Toronto and were granted a 10-day visitor visa, staying at the King Edward Hotel. They ultimately chose Montreal over Toronto for their bed-in because of its proximity to New York, which would facilitate easier American press coverage. "The choice was between Montreal and Toronto, and ultimately they chose Montreal because it was close to New York, which would make American press coverage much easier."

podcast.title: Toronto Rock and Roll Revival Performance (September 13, 1969)
podcast.body: John Lennon performed at Varsity Stadium in Toronto, facing severe stage fright and heroin withdrawal, as it was his first performance outside The Beatles. He was also intimidated by other acts on the bill, including his idols Chuck Berry, Gene Vincent, and Little Richard. "This was the first time John had ever performed outside the Beatles, which at the time were still a going concern."

This travel restriction was a key factor in his decision to host the bed-in in Montreal instead. "But due to a 1968 cannabis conviction, Lennon was not allowed in the United States."

podcast.title: Woodstock Performance Prohibited (1969)
podcast.body: John Lennon was originally scheduled to perform at the Woodstock festival but was ultimately prohibited from entering the United States. This ban was due to declarations he had made against the American government's policies and the ongoing war. "John Lennon originariamente iba a actuar en el festival de Gustock, finalmente nunca actuó, porque John Lennon le fue prohibida la entrada a los Estados Unidos por algunas de las declaraciones que había hecho en contra de las políticas del gobierno americano y en contra de la guerra."

podcast.title: Ann Arbor John Sinclair Freedom Rally (1971)
podcast.body: On December 10th, 1971, John and Yoko performed at a concert in Ann Arbor, Michigan, to support musician and activist John Sinclair, who was sentenced to 9.5-10 years for selling marijuana to undercover officers. The event, which also featured Stevie Wonder, Bob Seger, Allen Ginsberg, Bobby Seale, and Jerry Rubin, cost $3 for admission and was broadcast on Michigan radio. An article in the *New York Daily News* highlighted the event's "immediate inescapable impact" regarding the "potential power of the new young voter," and remarkably, John Sinclair was set free the following Monday morning. "John and Yoko performed at a concert in Ann Arbor, Michigan that was on behalf of Johnson Claire, a local musician and a political activist who happened to make the very unfortunate decision to sell marijuana to two undercover police officers."

podcast.title: Planned Anti-Nixon Tour (1972)
podcast.body: John Lennon planned an ambitious anti-Richard Nixon tour for 1972, intending to follow the President around the country and conclude with a three-day music festival outside the Republican National Convention in Miami. This plan, however, never materialized as Lennon's legal troubles and the attention of the FBI, instigated by Senator Strom Thurmond, led to a deportation attempt. "He thought, you know, maybe I could do a tour. An anti-Richard Nixon tour in 1972 and follow Richard Nixon around the country."

podcast.title: Hotel Suite Renamed and Renovated (1991, Recently)
podcast.body: In 1991, the Queen Elizabeth Hotel received permission from Yoko Ono to begin renting room 1742 in John Lennon's name. More recently, all four rooms (1738, 1740, 1742, and 1744) where the couple stayed were combined into one large suite, featuring two bedrooms, a dining room, two lounges, two bathrooms, a pantry, and virtual reality goggles to experience the view from Lennon's perspective. Today, this renovated suite is known as the "John Lennon and Yoko Ono suite." "Years later, in 1991, the Hotel received permission from Yoko Ono to begin renting room 1742 in Lenin's name."

podcast.title: Accidental Feedback Discovery
podcast.body: On October 18, 1964, while at Abbey Road Studios, John Lennon accidentally discovered the controlled feedback sound used on "I Feel Fine." After Paul McCartney plucked a bass string, John leaned his semi-acoustic Gibson guitar against Paul's bass amp and began to walk away, inadvertently causing the guitar to pick up the bass note and create feedback. Recognizing the unique sound, both Lennon and McCartney asked producer George Martin to capture it for their new song. "But then the guitar picked up the sound of that bass note and started feeding back, and the sound was really cool, but a total accident."

podcast.title: Assassination in New York City
podcast.body: John Lennon, the most famous member of The Beatles, was murdered on Monday, December 8, 1980, outside his apartment building on the west side of New York City. He was shot twice in the back and rushed to Roosevelt Hospital, where he was pronounced dead on arrival. "John Lennon, outside of his apartment building on the west side of New York City. The most famous, perhaps, of all of the Beatles. Shot twice in the back, rushed to Roosevelt Hospital dead on arrival."

podcast.body: Christine McVie's musical approach is described as having elements of John Lennon's bluesy rock, though neither Lennon's nor Paul McCartney's styles fully capture her unique skill. This comparison highlights a shared foundational genre influence. "She has elements of John Lenin's bluesy rock and Paul McCartney's melodicism."

podcast.title: Chuck Berry's Legacy Quote
podcast.body: John Lennon famously encapsulated Chuck Berry's monumental influence on music by stating, "if you tried to give rock and roll another name, it would be Chook Barry." This quote highlights Berry's indispensable and foundational role in the genre. "John Lennon once said, if you tried to give rock and roll another name, it would be Chook Barry, and for both better and worse, that's probably true."

podcast.title: Claimed Invention of Heavy Metal
podcast.body: John Lennon claimed that The Beatles' song "Ticket to Ride" from 1965 invented Heavy Metal. While not sounding "metal" on the surface, it is recognized as one of the earliest rock songs to use a guitar riff as its foundational element. "Not only that, but John claimed to have invented Heavy Metal with the Beatles song Ticket to Ride in 1965."

podcast.title: Collaboration with Bowie on "Young Americans"
podcast.body: John Lennon collaborated with David Bowie during his "last week in the Strangement" from Yoko Ono, co-writing the lyrics for the song "Fame" in about 20 minutes. He also provided background vocals, notably echoing the word "fame" in the verses of the recording for Bowie's "Young Americans" album. Lennon and Bowie got along famously, and Lennon's assistant, May Pang, later married Bowie's producer, Tony Visconti. "Not only did he and Bowie get along famously but so did Lennon's assistant May Pang and Bowie producer Tony Viscante and they actually ended up getting married."

podcast.title: Crater Lennon on Mercury
podcast.body: In December 2013, a crater approximately 95 kilometers in diameter on the planet Mercury was suggested for naming by the Messenger Spacecraft mission team. The International Astronomical Union (IAU) approved the suggestion, officially naming it Crater Lennon in honor of John Lennon. "In December 2013, the people running the Messenger Spacecraft on its mission to Mercury suggested that one crater about 95 kilometers in diameter be named after John Lennon, the IAU agreed, and now we have crater Lennon on Mercury."

podcast.title: Criticism of Paul McCartney's Solo Work
podcast.body: John Lennon was critical of Paul McCartney's post-Beatles musical output, calling it "too pop" and telling him, "You're all just pizza and fairy tales." Lennon's song "How Do You Sleep" was a direct attack on McCartney. However, Lennon himself released an album of oldies covers, like "Stand By Me" and "B-Bop-A-Lula," in 1975, which Andrew Grant Jackson noted suggested Lennon also had a "bit of pizza and fairy tales" in his own work. "Lenin took shots at McCartney's post Beatles work which he thought was all together to pop."

podcast.title: Exploring Emotional Vulnerability (Later Work)
podcast.body: John Lennon's musical output, several years after The Beach Boys' "Don't Worry Baby," ventured into similar territory by exploring emotional vulnerability, addressing "this very real area of the emotional landscape." Like Brian Wilson, Lennon frequently employed the motif of a "perfect woman" who acts as a savior for the protagonist in his songs. "Only some of John Lennon's work, a couple of years later, comes close to dealing with this very real area of the emotional landscape, and Lennon, like Wilson, often does so by using the figure of the perfect woman who will save the protagonist."

xref.title: Exemption from National Service (1957, 1960)
xref.body: The end of compulsory national service in Britain in 1957 (for those born after Oct 1, 1939) and its complete abolition in November 1960 meant that young men in bands like The Quarrymen were exempt from military service. This freedom allowed members like John Lennon (born October 1940) and Ringo Starr (born July 1940), and by implication, all four future Beatles, to continue pursuing music rather than being drafted. "And that meant that the young men in a new group called the Corrie men wouldn't have to worry about going into the army, so they kept at it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exemption from National Service (1957, 1960)
xref.body: All four members of The Beatles managed to avoid compulsory national service in Britain, which ended in 1957 for those born on or after October 1, 1939, and was completely abolished in November 1960. John Lennon (born October 1940) and Ringo Starr (born July 1940) were specifically mentioned as being exempt. This allowed them and countless other young British men to dedicate their time to forming bands and playing music, directly contributing to the explosion of the British music scene and the British Invasion. "And in November 1960, when compulsory service ended all together, all four members of the Beatles managed to avoid going into the army."

xref.title: 1958 Percy Phillips Home Recording – "That'll Be the Day" / "In Spite of All the Danger"
xref.body: An ultra-rare, two-sided 78 RPM disc from 1958, recorded by John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison, pianist John Lowe, and drummer Colin Hanton at the home of Percy Phillips, who specialized in "down and dirty" recordings in his front room. Side one features Buddy Holly's "That'll Be the Day," and side two contains "In Spite of All the Danger," the first-ever Lennon-McCartney recording. This record is owned by Paul McCartney and is estimated to be worth at least 100,000 pounds if it were ever to be sold. "The result was a two-sided 78 RPM disc with Buddy Holly's That'll Be the Day on Side One, and the first ever Lennon McCartney recording on the other, in spite of all the danger."

xref.title: John Lennon's Clash with Red Robinson (1964)
xref.body: Halfway through the Vancouver concert on August 22, 1964, as the crowd neared rioting, local radio host Red Robinson was instructed to go on stage to calm the fans. John Lennon, unaware of the situation, confronted Robinson, telling him, "Get off our stage, nobody interrupts the Beatles," before relenting after Robinson explained that manager Brian Epstein had sent him. "John looked down at Brian Epstein, the band's manager who gave him the okay. John turned Robinson and said, Okay, carry on mate."

xref.title: "More Popular Than Jesus" Controversy (1966)
xref.body: In 1966, John Lennon's casual comment that The Beatles were "more popular than Jesus" ignited a significant controversy. Broadcasters Tommy Charles and Doug Layton in Birmingham, Alabama, initiated a campaign to ban The Beatles over this perceived blasphemy, leading to numerous records being broken and publicly burned. "And when John Lennon made a flippin' comment in 1966 about the Beatles being more popular than Jesus, two broadcasters, Tommy Charles and Doug Layton from Birmingham, Alabama, started a campaign to ban the Beatles over this blasphemy, and many records were broken and burned."

xref.title: Montreal Bed-In for Peace (1969)
xref.body: Yoko Ono and her partner John Lennon held a week-long non-violent "bed-in for peace" protest in Montreal from May 26 to June 1, 1969, as a novel form of activism against the Vietnam War. This event was a successor to their Amsterdam bed-in and was relocated to Montreal after Lennon was denied entry to the US and a brief, uncomfortable stay in the Bahamas. "On May 26th, June 1st, 1969, he held a bed in for peace protest in Montreal."

xref.title: "The Eggman" Nickname Origin
xref.body: Eric Burdon, the leader of The Animals, acquired the nickname "the Eggman" after he disclosed details of an unusual oral sex act involving raw eggs, which he learned from his Jamaican girlfriend, Sylvia. This anecdote later found its way into The Beatles' song "I Am the Walrus," with John Lennon adopting the moniker. "And when he told everybody about it, he was immediately nicknamed the Eggman."

xref.title: Accidental Feedback Discovery
xref.body: On October 18, 1964, during a recording session at Abbey Road Studios, Paul McCartney accidentally initiated the controlled feedback sound that would be used on "I Feel Fine." He plucked a string on his bass, and when John Lennon laid his semi-acoustic Gibson guitar against Paul's bass amp, the guitar picked up the bass note and started feeding back. Paul and John recognized the coolness of the sound and requested producer George Martin to record it. "The discovery began when Paul McCarty picked a string on his bass, Appropole of Nothing, and then John laid his semi-acoustic Gibson guitar against Paul's bass amp and started to walk away."

xref.title: Assassination at El Rosa Villa Concert
xref.body: Dimebag Darrell, a revered guitarist from Pantera and Damageplan, was assassinated on December 8, 2004, exactly 24 years after John Lennon's death. During a Damageplan gig at the El Rosa Villa venue in Columbus, Ohio, attended by about 400 people, Nathan Gale rushed the stage and shot Darrell three times in the head at point-blank range as the band began their first song. "As the band started their first song at around 10-20 that night, a man named Nathan Gayle, 6'3", 250 pounds and wearing a Columbus Blue Jacket's hockey jersey, rushed the stage and shot Darryl with a 9mm semi-automatic pistol."

xref.title: Developing Mop Top Haircut (Astrid Kircher)
xref.body: About a year after the initial cut by Yurgen Volmer, during The Beatles' extended residency in Hamburg, Astrid Kircher regularly cut their hair into this new look. She first applied the cut to Stu Sutcliffe, then George Harrison, and finally John Lennon and Paul McCartney. Within two years, as The Beatles became the biggest band globally, their haircuts were nearly as famous as their music, solidifying long hair on men as a lasting trend. "She first gave the cut to Stu, and then George, and then finally John and Paul."

xref.body: Sean Lennon, the son of John Lennon and Yoko Ono, has had a varied musical career. xref.title: EMI Audition Demo (Undated) – "Hello Little Girl" / "Till There Was You" Acetate
xref.body: A one-of-a-kind, 10-inch acetate test pressing recorded as an audition for EMI Records, representing the first record featuring the Beatles as they would become known. Side A features "Hello Little Girl," credited to Paul McCartney and the Beatles, while Side B has "Till There Was You," credited to John Lennon and the Beatles; manager Brian Epstein wrote the titles in blue pen to ensure fairness. This record disappeared for decades before being found in the attic of Les Maguire, a member of Gerry and the Pacemakers. It was sold in March 2016 for 77,500 pounds, equivalent to $95,000 American or $130,000 Canadian. "It's a 10-inch acetate, a test pressing in other words, and is a one-of-a-kind thing Hello Little Girl on the A side, and Till There Was You on the B side."

xref.title: Origin of Mop Top Haircut (Yurgen Volmer)
xref.body: In 1961, Paul McCartney and John Lennon met Yurgen Volmer in Paris, who was a friend of Astrid Kircher and Stu Sutcliffe. Volmer had long hair parted and worn over his forehead, which "entranced" Lennon and McCartney, who still wore their hair slicked back. They asked him to cut their hair in his style, giving birth to the first version of the Beatles' mop top. "So he cut their hair, and so the Beatles' mop top was born, or at least the first version of it."

xref.title: Post-Breakup Media Feud
xref.body: After The Beatles broke up, Paul McCartney and John Lennon frequently engaged in public disputes through the media. "But after the Beatles broke up, Paul and John scrapped a lot in the media."

xref.title: Posthumous Impact and Legacy
xref.body: After his death, Kurt's image elevated him to the status of icons like Elvis, Buddy Holly, John Lennon, and Tupac, profoundly influencing rock, pop, and even hip-hop through his music, attitude, and image. "From that point on, Kurt was up there with Elvis, and Buddy Holly, and John Lennon, and Tupac."

xref.title: Ringo Starr's Gregarious Nature
xref.body: Bob Burns, the CJAYTV reporter who announced The Beatles' arrival in Winnipeg and interviewed John Lennon, later stated that Ringo Starr was the most gregarious member of the band and appeared to be the most mature. "He would later state that Ringo Star was the most gregarious of the band and seemed the most mature."

xref.title: Views on Heroin Culture
xref.body: Weiland openly admitted his love and intrigue for heroin culture, referencing influences from William S. Burroughs, Charlie Parker, the aesthetic of The Rolling Stones, John Lennon's heroin period, and the mid-80s impact of Perry Farrell and Jane's Addiction. He associated heroin with romance, glamour, danger, and rock and roll excess, and was curious about its connection to creativity. "The truth is that I loved heroin culture."
